Asunder
a-SUN-der
adverb
Saxon on sundran, apart, into separate parts — whence also sunder and sundry. In the Authorized Version it renders several Hebrew and Greek verbs of cleaving, parting, and breaking, always with the sense of a thing divided that was one.

Biblical Definition

Asunder always presupposes a union, and Scripture uses it to mark four kinds of parting. There is the parting God forbids: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6) — our Lord’s word on marriage, which grounds the permanence of the bond not in the feelings of the couple nor in the law of the state but in the act of God who joined them. There is the parting God performs in judgment, as when the ground clave asunder under Korah (Num 16:31), and in glory, as when the chariot of fire parted Elijah and Elisha asunder (2Ki 2:11). There is the parting rebellious man attempts against God: “Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us” (Psa 2:3) — the nations raging against the LORD and His Anointed, straining at cords they take for bondage and which are in truth the only thing holding them back from ruin. And there is the parting the word of God accomplishes within a man: “piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit” (Heb 4:12), a blade that separates what no other instrument can distinguish and lays the thoughts and intents of the heart open. Note which unions God defends and which He divides. He fences the marriage bond and cleaves the self-deceived heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Apart; into parts; in a divided state. In Scripture, the word of separation — forbidden in marriage, executed in judgment, attempted in rebellion, and performed by the word within the soul.

expand to see more

ASUNDER, adv. Apart; into parts; separately; in a divided state.

Saxon on sundran, apart; of the same root as sunder and sundry.

To cut, break, or cleave asunder, is to divide what was joined.

Of a bond dissolved: break their bands asunder (Psa 2:3).

Of discernment: the dividing asunder of soul and spirit (Heb 4:12).

Key Scripture

Psa 2:3 — "Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us."

2Ki 2:11 — "And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven."

Mat 19:6 — "Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

Heb 4:12 — "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart."

Modern Corruption

Mat 19:6 is the single most widely disregarded sentence of our Lord in the modern church — marriage is treated as a contract the parties may dissolve at will, when Christ grounds it in an act of God that no man is competent to undo.

expand to see more

The corruption is the reduction of marriage to private contract. If the bond is merely an agreement between two adults, then it may plainly be ended by the same two adults, and the only questions left are procedural — how quickly, how cheaply, how amicably. Our Lord cuts that reasoning off at the root. He does not appeal to social utility, to the good of children, or even to the vows exchanged; He appeals to the act of God: what God hath joined together. The joining is His work, done at the wedding whether or not the couple knew it, and the prohibition follows necessarily — no man may put asunder what he did not join. The permanence is not a heavy expectation laid upon the couple’s endurance; it is a statement about who tied the knot.

Recover the plain sense: the same sentence that binds the married comforts them. A bond that rests on the act of God does not hang by the thread of present affection, and a Christian may therefore work at a hard marriage as a man works on a house he cannot be evicted from. Set Mat 19:6 beside Heb 4:12 and the pastoral order appears. God defends the union He made between husband and wife, and He divides the union a man has made between his flattering self-estimate and the truth. We commonly want it the other way — a searching word for our marriages and a gentle one for our hearts. Scripture gives the sword to the heart and the shield to the marriage.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon on sundran, apart — separation, forbidden where God has joined and performed where God discerns.

expand to see more

Asunder — Saxon on sundran, apart, in separate parts.

Kin to sunder, sundry, and the German besonders.

Of judgment: the ground clave asunder beneath Korah (Num 16:31).

Of marriage: forbidden to man because the joining was God’s act (Mat 19:6).

Of the word: it divides soul and spirit, which no other blade can part (Heb 4:12).

Usage

"Mat 19:6 rests the permanence of marriage on God’s joining, not the couple’s resolve."

"Psa 2:3: the cords the nations strain against are mercy, not bondage."

"Heb 4:12 turns the word into a blade that divides what a man cannot divide in himself."
